title: Pristinia · a town worth defending
dek: Arrival, shared defenses, siege and the ordinary work that makes survival matter.

facts.Dates: Source chronology; uncertain intervals remain explicit

body:
The history of Pristinia follows a change in obligation. People arrive needing orientation and protection; they build institutions that others will depend on. Its wars matter because a town of meals, homes, work and memory stands inside the defenses.

A name before a settled identity

In the early naming exchange, Jiangshi proposes Pristinia; Melian favors the name while questioning John’s grander wording for a small settlement. The future city is still an aspiration. This exchange keeps several voices in its beginning rather than making the name the inevitable expression of one founder’s vision.

Scribonia’s early notes describe what he thinks the settlement lacks and record travel information attributed to the Master Librarian. Those notes tell us what an arrival tried to understand. Their subjective development rank does not replace the inhabitants already there or create an official classification. The original notes and the naming scene answer different questions.

The Gate makes arrival a recurring civic task. Later, Tobias offers Fredrick food and points him toward Herb’s rations. New arrivals depend on people such as Tobias and Herb for food and directions.

Defenses built by many hands

The wall belongs to a history of distributed labor. Ryvyt describes following other builders and using Mending to reinforce their work and address hidden weaknesses. Repair is part of the defense, not an achievement that can be credited only to the people whose names appear in a later summary.

The Ale-Chemy Knights connect equipment, gathering, trade and personal aid. Ryvyt’s later request for scouts shows a limit to craft: a skilled workshop still needs plants, relics, stone and metal. That request records a dependency on other people; it does not prove every requested delivery happened.

The town’s households, Scroll Library and Common Man make defense consequential. Supplies, places to learn and people who remember one another are part of what can be lost. Their separate histories preserve the limits on ownership and exact transfers. The fire now has a direct quest chronology.

The siege makes vulnerability immediate

By the checked 29 May 2025 quest scene, catapult fire continues while the defenders debate. A boulder strikes a nearby house; reconnaissance locates the siege engines and ballista towers beyond the town. The threat is acting while the company makes decisions. Later knowledge of the campaign cannot be assigned to everyone in that moment.

The established siege history retains Elenia’s intervention against the towers and the public title Savior of Pristinia. A title records reputation; it does not remove the defenders, healers, firefighters and builders from the outcome. Nor does a single dated siege scene securely date every stage of the war.

The discovery at Melian’s house marks another crisis. Narration places Herb, Lillian and the raven dead nearby and Melian missing, and explicitly says the event happened the preceding day. The discovery gives the search a starting point; at that moment it does not reveal the attackers’ entire plan. Posting time, discovery and abduction must remain distinct.

Survival becomes a continuing responsibility

The later record returns to repair, remembrance, care and unfinished public work. The Pilgrim’s Hearth carries the history of a place where people ate and mourned, after the Common Man’s destruction in the quest scene posted 27–28 June 2026 (UTC). The complete casualty record remains open; rebuilding should not erase that loss.

Pristinia’s campaign therefore has no single founder, defender or final restorative act that can explain the whole settlement. The checked scenes support a more specific account: people name a home, reinforce it, discover its vulnerabilities and keep taking responsibility for it. The claim review separates those observations from larger claims still requiring proof.
